claim: TFIIH is a heterodecameric protein complex critical for transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II and nucleotide excision DNA repair.
source: Transcription factor IIH (TFIIH) is a heterodecameric protein complex critical for transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II and nucleotide excision DNA repair.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about TFIIH that draws from established scientific consensus about its composition and functions.

claim: The TFIIH core complex is sufficient for its repair functions.
source: The TFIIH core complex is sufficient for its repair functions and harbors the XPB and XPD DNA-dependent ATPase/helicase subunits, which are affected by human disease mutations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work (Svejstrup et al., 1995) mentioned later in the introduction.

claim: The TFIIH core complex harbors the XPB and XPD DNA-dependent ATPase/helicase subunits.
source: The TFIIH core complex is sufficient for its repair functions and harbors the XPB and XPD DNA-dependent ATPase/helicase subunits, which are affected by human disease mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of TFIIH core complex.

claim: XPB and XPD are affected by human disease mutations.
source: The TFIIH core complex is sufficient for its repair functions and harbors the XPB and XPD DNA-dependent ATPase/helicase subunits, which are affected by human disease mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Cleaver et al., 1999; Rapin, 2013).

claim: Transcription initiation additionally requires the CdK activating kinase subcomplex.
source: Transcription initiation additionally requires the CdK activating kinase subcomplex.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Devault et al., 1995; Fisher et al., 1995; Fisher and Morgan, 1994; Shiekhattar et al., 1995; Svejstrup et al., 1995) mentioned later in the text.

claim: The complete structure of the human TFIIH core complex was determined by phase-plate cryo-electron microscopy at 3.7 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present the complete structure of the human TFIIH core complex, determined by phase-plate cryo-electron microscopy at 3.7 Å resolution.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure uncovers the molecular basis of TFIIH assembly.
source: The structure uncovers the molecular basis of TFIIH assembly, revealing how the recruitment of XPB by p52 depends on a pseudo-symmetric dimer of homologous domains in these two proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The recruitment of XPB by p52 depends on a pseudo-symmetric dimer of homologous domains in these two proteins.
source: The structure uncovers the molecular basis of TFIIH assembly, revealing how the recruitment of XPB by p52 depends on a pseudo-symmetric dimer of homologous domains in these two proteins.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The structure suggests a function for p62 in the regulation of XPD.
source: The structure also suggests a function for p62 in the regulation of XPD, and allows the mapping of previously unresolved human disease mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of p62-XPD interactions shown in Figure 2.

claim: The structure allows the mapping of previously unresolved human disease mutations.
source: The structure also suggests a function for p62 in the regulation of XPD, and allows the mapping of previously unresolved human disease mutations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mapping of disease mutations onto the structure in Figure 6 and Appendix 2.

claim: TFIIH is a 10-subunit protein complex with a total molecular weight of 0.5 MDa.
source: Transcription factor IIH (TFIIH) is a 10-subunit protein complex with a total molecular weight of 0.5 MDa that serves a dual role as a general transcription factor for transcription initiation by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II (Pol II), and as a DNA helicase complex in nucleotide excision DNA repair (NER) (Compe and Egly, 2016; Sainsbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TFIIH serves a dual role as a general transcription factor for transcription initiation by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II and as a DNA helicase complex in nucleotide excision DNA repair.
source: Transcription factor IIH (TFIIH) is a 10-subunit protein complex with a total molecular weight of 0.5 MDa that serves a dual role as a general transcription factor for transcription initiation by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II (Pol II), and as a DNA helicase complex in nucleotide excision DNA repair (NER) (Compe and Egly, 2016; Sainsbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in TFIIH subunits cause the inherited autosomal recessive disorders xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), trichothiodystrophy (TTD), and Cockayne syndrome (CS).
source: Mutations in TFIIH subunits that cause the inherited autosomal recessive disorders xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), trichothiodystrophy (TTD), and Cockayne syndrome (CS) are characterized by high incidence of cancer or premature ageing (Cleaver et al., 1999; Rapin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutations in TFIIH subunits that cause XP, TTD, and CS are characterized by high incidence of cancer or premature ageing.
source: Mutations in TFIIH subunits that cause the inherited autosomal recessive disorders xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), trichothiodystrophy (TTD), and Cockayne syndrome (CS) are characterized by high incidence of cancer or premature ageing (Cleaver et al., 1999; Rapin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TFIIH is a possible target for anti-cancer compounds.
source: Furthermore, TFIIH is a possible target for anti-cancer compounds (Berico and Coin, 2018) and therefore of great importance for human health and disease.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The TFIIH core complex is composed of the seven subunits XPB, XPD, p62, p52, p44, p34, and p8.
source: The TFIIH core complex is composed of the seven subunits XPB, XPD, p62, p52, p44, p34, and p8, and is the form of TFIIH active in DNA repair (Svejstrup et al., 1995), where TFIIH serves as a DNA damage verification factor (Li et al., 2015; Mathieu et al., 2013) and is responsible for opening a repair bubble around damaged nucleotides.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The TFIIH core complex is the form of TFIIH active in DNA repair.
source: The TFIIH core complex is composed of the seven subunits XPB, XPD, p62, p52, p44, p34, and p8, and is the form of TFIIH active in DNA repair (Svejstrup et al., 1995), where TFIIH serves as a DNA damage verification factor (Li et al., 2015; Mathieu et al., 2013) and is responsible for opening a repair bubble around damaged nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: TFIIH serves as a DNA damage verification factor.
source: The TFIIH core complex is composed of the seven subunits XPB, XPD, p62, p52, p44, p34, and p8, and is the form of TFIIH active in DNA repair (Svejstrup et al., 1995), where TFIIH serves as a DNA damage verification factor (Li et al., 2015; Mathieu et al., 2013) and is responsible for opening a repair bubble around damaged nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: TFIIH is responsible for opening a repair bubble around damaged nucleotides.
source: The TFIIH core complex is composed of the seven subunits XPB, XPD, p62, p52, p44, p34, and p8, and is the form of TFIIH active in DNA repair (Svejstrup et al., 1995), where TFIIH serves as a DNA damage verification factor (Li et al., 2015; Mathieu et al., 2013) and is responsible for opening a repair bubble around damaged nucleotides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TFIIH function.

claim: TFIIH activity in DNA repair depends on both the SF2-family DNA-dependent ATPase XPB and the DNA helicase activity of XPD.
source: This activity depends on both the SF2-family DNA-dependent ATPase XPB, and the DNA helicase activity of XPD (Coin et al., 2007; Evans et al., 1997; Kuper et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: TFIIH function in transcription initiation requires the double-stranded DNA translocase activity of XPB to regulate opening of the transcription bubble.
source: TFIIH function in transcription initiation requires the double-stranded DNA translocase activity of XPB to regulate opening of the transcription bubble (Alekseev et al., 2017; Fishburn et al., 2015; Grünberg et al., 2012), and additionally the CdK activating kinase (CAK) complex, which harbors the kinase activity of CDK7 as well as the Cyclin H and MAT1 subunits (Devault et al., 1995; Fisher et al., 1995; Fisher and Morgan, 1994; Shiekhattar et al., 1995; Svejstrup et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The CAK complex harbors the kinase activity of CDK7 as well as the Cyclin H and MAT1 subunits.
source: TFIIH function in transcription initiation requires the double-stranded DNA translocase activity of XPB to regulate opening of the transcription bubble (Alekseev et al., 2017; Fishburn et al., 2015; Grünberg et al., 2012), and additionally the CdK activating kinase (CAK) complex, which harbors the kinase activity of CDK7 as well as the Cyclin H and MAT1 subunits (Devault et al., 1995; Fisher et al., 1995; Fisher and Morgan, 1994; Shiekhattar et al., 1995; Svejstrup et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Targets of human CDK7 include the C-terminal heptapeptide repeat domain of the largest subunit of Pol II.
source: Targets of human CDK7 include the C-terminal heptapeptide repeat domain of the largest subunit of Pol II, as well as cell-cycle regulating CDKs (Fisher and Morgan, 1994; Shiekhattar et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Targets of human CDK7 include cell-cycle regulating CDKs.
source: Targets of human CDK7 include the C-terminal heptapeptide repeat domain of the largest subunit of Pol II, as well as cell-cycle regulating CDKs (Fisher and Morgan, 1994; Shiekhattar et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MAT1 serves as a bridging subunit that promotes CAK subcomplex formation by interacting with Cyclin H and CDK7.
source: MAT1 serves as a bridging subunit that promotes CAK subcomplex formation by interacting with Cyclin H and CDK7 (Devault et al., 1995; Fisher et al., 1995), recruits the CAK to the core complex by interactions with XPD and XPB (Abdulrahman et al., 2013; Busso et al., 2000; Greber et al., 2017; Rossignol et al., 1997), and also aids in Pol II-PIC formation by establishing interactions with the core PIC (He et al., 2013; He et al., 2016; Schilbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MAT1 recruits the CAK to the core complex by interactions with XPD and XPB.
source: MAT1 serves as a bridging subunit that promotes CAK subcomplex formation by interacting with Cyclin H and CDK7 (Devault et al., 1995; Fisher et al., 1995), recruits the CAK to the core complex by interactions with XPD and XPB (Abdulrahman et al., 2013; Busso et al., 2000; Greber et al., 2017; Rossignol et al., 1997), and also aids in Pol II-PIC formation by establishing interactions with the core PIC (He et al., 2013; He et al., 2016; Schilbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MAT1 aids in Pol II-PIC formation by establishing interactions with the core PIC.
source: MAT1 serves as a bridging subunit that promotes CAK subcomplex formation by interacting with Cyclin H and CDK7 (Devault et al., 1995; Fisher et al., 1995), recruits the CAK to the core complex by interactions with XPD and XPB (Abdulrahman et al., 2013; Busso et al., 2000; Greber et al., 2017; Rossignol et al., 1997), and also aids in Pol II-PIC formation by establishing interactions with the core PIC (He et al., 2013; He et al., 2016; Schilbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The presence of MAT1 inhibits the helicase activity of XPD.
source: The presence of MAT1 inhibits the helicase activity of XPD (Abdulrahman et al., 2013; Sandrock and Egly, 2001), but the mechanism of this inhibition is not fully understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The enzymatic activity of XPD is not required for transcription initiation.
source: While the enzymatic activity of XPD is not required for transcription initiation, it is critical for the DNA repair function of TFIIH (Dubaele et al., 2003; Evans et al., 1997; Kuper et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The enzymatic activity of XPD is critical for the DNA repair function of TFIIH.
source: While the enzymatic activity of XPD is not required for transcription initiation, it is critical for the DNA repair function of TFIIH (Dubaele et al., 2003; Evans et al., 1997; Kuper et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: NER requires the release of the CAK subcomplex from the core complex.
source: Therefore, NER requires the release of the CAK subcomplex from the core complex (Coin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The activities of both XPB and XPD are regulated by interactions with additional TFIIH components.
source: The activities of both XPB and XPD are regulated by interactions with additional TFIIH components, including that of p44 with XPD (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2015), and those of the p52-p8 module with XPB (Coin et al., 2007; Coin et al., 2006; Jawhari et al., 2002; Kainov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: p44 regulates XPD activity.
source: The activities of both XPB and XPD are regulated by interactions with additional TFIIH components, including that of p44 with XPD (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2015), and those of the p52-p8 module with XPB (Coin et al., 2007; Coin et al., 2006; Jawhari et al., 2002; Kainov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The p52-p8 module regulates XPB activity.
source: The activities of both XPB and XPD are regulated by interactions with additional TFIIH components, including that of p44 with XPD (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2015), and those of the p52-p8 module with XPB (Coin et al., 2007; Coin et al., 2006; Jawhari et al., 2002; Kainov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Some interactions regulating XPB and XPD are affected by disease mutations.
source: These interactions are likely to be crucial for TFIIH function, as some are affected by disease mutations (Cleaver et al., 1999), but they have been only partially characterized mechanistically.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The previous structure of the TFIIH core-MAT1 complex was at 4.4 Å resolution.
source: Our previous structure of the TFIIH core-MAT1 complex at 4.4 Å resolution (Greber et al., 2017) allowed modeling of TFIIH in the best-resolved parts of the density map, but several functionally important regions remained unassigned or only partially interpreted because reliable de novo tracing of entire domains in the absence of existing structural models was not possible.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: Several functionally important regions remained unassigned or only partially interpreted in the previous 4.4 Å structure.
source: Our previous structure of the TFIIH core-MAT1 complex at 4.4 Å resolution (Greber et al., 2017) allowed modeling of TFIIH in the best-resolved parts of the density map, but several functionally important regions remained unassigned or only partially interpreted because reliable de novo tracing of entire domains in the absence of existing structural models was not possible.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous work.

claim: The cryo-EM maps define the molecular contacts that control the regulation of the XPB and XPD subunits of TFIIH.
source: Additionally, our cryo-EM maps define the molecular contacts that control the regulation of the XPB and XPD subunits of TFIIH, including the critical p52-XBP interaction, and an extensive regulatory network around XPD, formed by XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An extensive regulatory network around XPD is formed by XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1.
source: Additionally, our cryo-EM maps define the molecular contacts that control the regulation of the XPB and XPD subunits of TFIIH, including the critical p52-XBP interaction, and an extensive regulatory network around XPD, formed by XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TFIIH was immuno-purified from HeLa cells.
source: To determine the complete structure of the human TFIIH core complex, we collected several large cryo-EM datasets (Supplementary file 1) of TFIIH immuno-purified from HeLa cells using an electron microscope equipped with a Volta phase plate (VPP) (Danev and Baumeister, 2017) and a direct electron detector camera mounted behind an energy filter.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: A 3D cryo-EM density map was reconstructed from approximately 140,000 TFIIH particle images.
source: From a homogeneous subset of approximately 140,000 TFIIH particle images identified by 3D classification (Scheres, 2010), we reconstructed a 3D cryo-EM density map at 3.7 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2A–C).
evidence: This describes the data processing and reconstruction.

claim: The VPP-based cryo-EM map was substantially improved compared to previous maps obtained without phase plate.
source: This VPP-based cryo-EM map was substantially improved compared to our previous maps obtained without phase plate, both in resolution and interpretability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G), and enabled building, refinement, and full validation of an atomic model of the TFIIH core complex and the MAT1 subunit of the CAK subcomplex (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C, Supplementary file 2, 3), while the remainder of the CAK subcomplex is invisible in our map because it is flexibly tethered to the TFIIH core complex.
evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: The remainder of the CAK subcomplex is invisible in the cryo-EM map because it is flexibly tethered to the TFIIH core complex.
source: This VPP-based cryo-EM map was substantially improved compared to our previous maps obtained without phase plate, both in resolution and interpretability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G), and enabled building, refinement, and full validation of an atomic model of the TFIIH core complex and the MAT1 subunit of the CAK subcomplex (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C, Supplementary file 2, 3), while the remainder of the CAK subcomplex is invisible in our map because it is flexibly tethered to the TFIIH core complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of density in the map.

claim: Tracing and sequence register assignment of protein components modeled de novo was facilitated by density maps obtained from focused classification and multibody refinement.
source: Tracing and sequence register assignment of protein components modeled de novo was facilitated by density maps obtained from focused classification and multibody refinement (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5) (Bai et al., 2015; Nakane et al., 2018), which resulted in density maps of improved interpretability for all three sub-volumes and a slightly improved resolution of 3.6 Å for the XPD-MAT1 region.
evidence: This describes the methods used for model building.

claim: Multibody refinement resulted in a slightly improved resolution of 3.6 Å for the XPD-MAT1 region.
source: Tracing and sequence register assignment of protein components modeled de novo was facilitated by density maps obtained from focused classification and multibody refinement (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5) (Bai et al., 2015; Nakane et al., 2018), which resulted in density maps of improved interpretability for all three sub-volumes and a slightly improved resolution of 3.6 Å for the XPD-MAT1 region.
evidence: This is a result from the data processing.

claim: The overall and multibody-refined maps showed clear side chain information.
source: Both the overall and multibody-refined maps showed clear side chain information (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–D.

claim: The model was corroborated by existing chemical crosslinking-mass spectrometry (CX-MS) data of human TFIIH.
source: Furthermore, our model was corroborated by existing chemical crosslinking-mass spectrometry (CX-MS) data of human TFIIH (Luo et al., 2015) and site-specific crosslinks from yeast TFIIH (Warfield et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E–I, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published CX-MS data.

claim: The structure of the TFIIH core complex shows its horseshoe-like overall shape.
source: Our structure of the TFIIH core complex shows its horseshoe-like overall shape (Figure 1A–C, Video 1), as observed in previous lower-resolution reconstructions of free and PIC-bound TFIIH (Gibbons et al., 2012; Greber et al., 2017; He et al., 2016; Murakami et al., 2015; Schilbach et al., 2017), and allows us to define the complete set of inter-subunit interactions that lead to the formation of the TFIIH core complex directly from our structure (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and shown in Figure 1A–C.

claim: The horseshoe-like shape was observed in previous lower-resolution reconstructions of free and PIC-bound TFIIH.
source: Our structure of the TFIIH core complex shows its horseshoe-like overall shape (Figure 1A–C, Video 1), as observed in previous lower-resolution reconstructions of free and PIC-bound TFIIH (Gibbons et al., 2012; Greber et al., 2017; He et al., 2016; Murakami et al., 2015; Schilbach et al., 2017), and allows us to define the complete set of inter-subunit interactions that lead to the formation of the TFIIH core complex directly from our structure (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: XPB and XPD both contain two RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2).
source: The largest subunits of the complex, the SF2-family DNA-dependent ATPases XPB and XPD, both containing two RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2), interact directly (Greber et al., 2017), are on one side of the complex, and are additionally bridged by MAT1 (Figure 1B), which has been shown to interact with either ATPase in isolation (Busso et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of these proteins.

claim: XPB and XPD interact directly.
source: The largest subunits of the complex, the SF2-family DNA-dependent ATPases XPB and XPD, both containing two RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2), interact directly (Greber et al., 2017), are on one side of the complex, and are additionally bridged by MAT1 (Figure 1B), which has been shown to interact with either ATPase in isolation (Busso et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: XPB and XPD are additionally bridged by MAT1.
source: The largest subunits of the complex, the SF2-family DNA-dependent ATPases XPB and XPD, both containing two RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2), interact directly (Greber et al., 2017), are on one side of the complex, and are additionally bridged by MAT1 (Figure 1B), which has been shown to interact with either ATPase in isolation (Busso et al., 2000).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MAT1 has been shown to interact with either XPB or XPD in isolation.
source: The largest subunits of the complex, the SF2-family DNA-dependent ATPases XPB and XPD, both containing two RecA-like domains (RecA1 and RecA2), interact directly (Greber et al., 2017), are on one side of the complex, and are additionally bridged by MAT1 (Figure 1B), which has been shown to interact with either ATPase in isolation (Busso et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: XPD interacts with the von Willebrand Factor A (vWFA) domain of p44.
source: On the side facing away from MAT1, XPD interacts with the von Willebrand Factor A (vWFA) domain of p44 (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; He et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015), which in turn forms a tight interaction with p34 via interlocking eZnF domains (Schilbach et al., 2017) and a p44 RING domain interaction (Radu et al., 2017) (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6J,K), consistent with the formation of a multivalent interaction network between p34 and p44 (Radu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: p44 forms a tight interaction with p34 via interlocking eZnF domains.
source: On the side facing away from MAT1, XPD interacts with the von Willebrand Factor A (vWFA) domain of p44 (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; He et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015), which in turn forms a tight interaction with p34 via interlocking eZnF domains (Schilbach et al., 2017) and a p44 RING domain interaction (Radu et al., 2017) (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6J,K), consistent with the formation of a multivalent interaction network between p34 and p44 (Radu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: p44 forms a p44 RING domain interaction with p34.
source: On the side facing away from MAT1, XPD interacts with the von Willebrand Factor A (vWFA) domain of p44 (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; He et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015), which in turn forms a tight interaction with p34 via interlocking eZnF domains (Schilbach et al., 2017) and a p44 RING domain interaction (Radu et al., 2017) (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6J,K), consistent with the formation of a multivalent interaction network between p34 and p44 (Radu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: A multivalent interaction network exists between p34 and p44.
source: On the side facing away from MAT1, XPD interacts with the von Willebrand Factor A (vWFA) domain of p44 (Coin et al., 1998; Dubaele et al., 2003; He et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015), which in turn forms a tight interaction with p34 via interlocking eZnF domains (Schilbach et al., 2017) and a p44 RING domain interaction (Radu et al., 2017) (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6J,K), consistent with the formation of a multivalent interaction network between p34 and p44 (Radu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The vWFA domain of p34 recruits p52 by a three-way interaction that involves the most N-terminal winged helix domain in p52 and a helical segment of p62.
source: The vWFA domain of p34 recruits p52 by a three-way interaction that involves the most N-terminal winged helix domain in p52 and a helical segment of p62 (Schilbach et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6L).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The p52 C-terminal region comprises two domains: the 'clutch' that interacts with XPB and a dimerization module that binds p8.
source: The p52 C-terminal region comprises two domains; first, the 'clutch' that interacts with XPB (Jawhari et al., 2002) and second, a dimerization module that binds p8 (Kainov et al., 2008), thereby recruiting XPB to TFIIH and cradling XPB RecA2 (see below).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 15 residues of p44 span the distance between the p44 vWFA domain and the XPB NTD.
source: To form this interaction, approx. 15 residues of p44 span the distance between the p44 vWFA domain and the XPB NTD, where a small helical motif in p44 contacts XPB residues 72–75, 95–102, and 139–143, in agreement with CX-MS data (Luo et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by CX-MS data.

claim: A small helical motif in p44 contacts XPB residues 72–75, 95–102, and 139–143.
source: To form this interaction, approx. 15 residues of p44 span the distance between the p44 vWFA domain and the XPB NTD, where a small helical motif in p44 contacts XPB residues 72–75, 95–102, and 139–143, in agreement with CX-MS data (Luo et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by CX-MS data.

claim: Partial deletion of the p44 NTE in yeast causes a slow-growth phenotype.
source: Partial deletion of the p44 NTE in yeast causes a slow-growth phenotype, suggesting a functional role for this p44-XPB interaction (Warfield et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: p62 is almost completely resolved in the structure.
source: The p62 subunit is almost completely resolved in our structure and exhibits a complex beads-on-a-string-like topology.
evidence: This is a description of the structural data.

claim: p62 exhibits a complex beads-on-a-string-like topology.
source: The p62 subunit is almost completely resolved in our structure and exhibits a complex beads-on-a-string-like topology.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: p62 fully encircles the top surface of TFIIH.
source: It fully encircles the top surface of TFIIH (Figures 1C and 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), interacting with XPD, p52, p44, and p34, in agreement with previous structural findings (Greber et al., 2017; Schilbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: p62 interacts with XPD, p52, p44, and p34.
source: It fully encircles the top surface of TFIIH (Figures 1C and 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), interacting with XPD, p52, p44, and p34, in agreement with previous structural findings (Greber et al., 2017; Schilbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminal PH-domain of p62 is disordered in the structure.
source: Based on these interactions, p62 can be subdivided into three functional regions: (i) the N-terminal PH-domain, disordered in our structure, is responsible for mediating interactions with components of the core transcriptional machinery (Di Lello et al., 2008; He et al., 2016; Schilbach et al., 2017), transcriptional regulators (Di Lello et al., 2006), and DNA repair pathways (Gervais et al., 2004; Lafrance-Vanasse et al., 2013; Okuda et al., 2017); (ii) residues 108–148 and 454–548 of p62, including the first BSD (BTF2-like, synapse-associated, DOS2-like) domain (BSD1) and the C-terminal 3-helix bundle, play an architectural role by binding to p34 and the extended zinc finger (eZnF) domain of p44 (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 6J–L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C); and (iii) residues 160–365, including the BSD2 domain, are responsible for interactions with and regulation of XPD (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The N-terminal PH-domain of p62 is responsible for mediating interactions with components of the core transcriptional machinery.

claim: The cryo-EM map shows side-chain densities for the aromatic residues Y158, F161, and F193 in the XPD FeS domain.
source: This region was poorly defined in previous TFIIH reconstructions, but our cryo-EM map now shows side-chain densities for the aromatic residues Y158, F161, and F193, which are critical for the DNA-binding, ATPase, and helicase activities of XPD (Kuper et al., 2014), as well as for residues Y192 and R196, which form part of a DNA lesion recognition pocket (Mathieu et al., 2013) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Y158, F161, and F193 are critical for the DNA-binding, ATPase, and helicase activities of XPD.
source: This region was poorly defined in previous TFIIH reconstructions, but our cryo-EM map now shows side-chain densities for the aromatic residues Y158, F161, and F193, which are critical for the DNA-binding, ATPase, and helicase activities of XPD (Kuper et al., 2014), as well as for residues Y192 and R196, which form part of a DNA lesion recognition pocket (Mathieu et al., 2013) (Figure 5B).

claim: The functionally important region around the XPD FeS domain is only partially conserved in archaeal XPD homologs.
source: This functionally important region is only partially conserved in archaeal XPD homologs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I) (Fan et al., 2008; Kuper et al., 2012; Wolski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in sequence alignments and supported by citations.

claim: A eukaryotic-specific loop insertion in the XPD ARCH domain closely approaches the lesion recognition pocket.
source: A eukaryotic-specific loop insertion in the XPD ARCH domain (Greber et al., 2017; Schilbach et al., 2017) closely approaches this binding pocket (Figure 5B) and may serve to regulate the binding of DNA in the lesion recognition pocket such as to prevent untimely access of substrates to the XPD pore.
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The eukaryotic-specific loop insertion in the XPD ARCH domain may serve to regulate the binding of DNA in the lesion recognition pocket.
source: A eukaryotic-specific loop insertion in the XPD ARCH domain (Greber et al., 2017; Schilbach et al., 2017) closely approaches this binding pocket (Figure 5B) and may serve to regulate the binding of DNA in the lesion recognition pocket such as to prevent untimely access of substrates to the XPD pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: XPD forms architectural and regulatory interactions with four other TFIIH subunits: XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1.
source: Our structure of TFIIH shows that XPD forms architectural and regulatory interactions with four other TFIIH subunits: XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1, which together form a cradle-like structure around XPD (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1 together form a cradle-like structure around XPD.
source: Our structure of TFIIH shows that XPD forms architectural and regulatory interactions with four other TFIIH subunits: XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1, which together form a cradle-like structure around XPD (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The helicase activity of XPD is inhibited by the CAK subcomplex.
source: Additionally, it is known that the helicase activity of XPD is inhibited by the CAK subcomplex (Araújo et al., 2000; Sandrock and Egly, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The contacts between MAT1 and XPD localize to the ARCH domain of XPD and the N-terminal RING domain and helical bundle of MAT1.
source: The contacts we see between MAT1 and XPD localize to the ARCH domain of XPD and the N-terminal RING domain and helical bundle of MAT1 (residues 1–130) (Figure 5C), in agreement with previous structural (Greber et al., 2017; Schilbach et al., 2017) and biochemical analysis (Abdulrahman et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2015; Warfield et al., 2016).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between the XPD ARCH domain and the MAT1 helical bundle is characterized by charge complementarity.
source: The interaction between the XPD ARCH domain and the MAT1 helical bundle is characterized by charge complementarity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The MAT1-XPD interface is highly dynamic, enabling the release of MAT1 and the entire CAK subcomplex from TFIIH during NER.
source: This interface is highly dynamic, enabling the release of MAT1 and the entire CAK subcomplex from TFIIH during NER, as well as its subsequent re-association to regenerate a transcription-competent TFIIH (Coin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and supported by a citation.

claim: Insertion of substrate DNA into the pore between the XPD ARCH and FeS domains requires the flexibility of the XPD ARCH domain.
source: Insertion of substrate DNA into the pore between the XPD ARCH and FeS domains requires the flexibility of the XPD ARCH domain (Constantinescu-Aruxandei et al., 2016), and large domain motions have been observed in the structure of the DNA-bound homologous helicase DinG upon nucleotide binding (Cheng and Wigley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Large domain motions have been observed in the structure of the DNA-bound homologous helicase DinG upon nucleotide binding.
source: Insertion of substrate DNA into the pore between the XPD ARCH and FeS domains requires the flexibility of the XPD ARCH domain (Constantinescu-Aruxandei et al., 2016), and large domain motions have been observed in the structure of the DNA-bound homologous helicase DinG upon nucleotide binding (Cheng and Wigley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The mobility of the ARCH domain plays a role in both DNA loading and DNA translocation by the XPD helicase.
source: This suggests a role for the mobility of the ARCH domain in both DNA loading and DNA translocation by the XPD helicase.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and comparison with DinG.

claim: Binding of the MAT1 helical bundle and RING domain to the ARCH domain may prevent motion of the ARCH domain and therefore subsequent substrate loading and XPD helicase activity.
source: Our structure suggests that binding of the MAT1 helical bundle and RING domain to the ARCH domain may prevent such motion and therefore the subsequent substrate loading and XPD helicase activity (Figure 5D), in agreement with biochemical data that show XPD inhibition upon MAT1 binding (Sandrock and Egly, 2001), as well as reduced single-stranded DNA affinity of TFIIH in the presence of the CAK (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and supported by citations.

claim: Release of MAT1 from XPD might allow the ARCH domain to move more freely, thereby de-repressing XPD.
source: Conversely, release of MAT1 from XPD might allow the ARCH domain to move more freely, thereby de-repressing XPD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Displacement of the MAT1 α-helix that connects XPD to XPB may allow XPB to move away from XPD, thereby unmasking the substrate-binding site on XPD RecA2.
source: Furthermore, displacement of the MAT1 α-helix that connects XPD to XPB may allow XPB to move away from XPD, thereby unmasking the substrate-binding site on XPD RecA2 that is otherwise occluded by the DRD insertion element (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The conformational change allowing XPB to move away from XPD would be similar to that seen for TFIIH upon incorporation into the Pol II-PIC.
source: This latter conformational change would be similar, overall, to that seen for TFIIH upon incorporation into the Pol II-PIC, where XPD and XPB move apart and density for the MAT1 helix is missing (Figure 4C) (He et al., 2016; Schilbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with PIC structures.

claim: The combined unmasking of the XPD substrate binding site and the enhanced flexibility of the XPD ARCH domain may both contribute to de-repression of the XPD helicase upon release of MAT1.
source: We propose that the combined unmasking of the XPD substrate binding site and the enhanced flexibility of the XPD ARCH domain may both contribute to de-repression of the XPD helicase upon release of MAT1.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the structural observations.

claim: This mechanism of XPD inhibition by MAT1 does not exclude the possibility of additional repression of NER activity by the CAK subcomplex through phosphorylation of NER pathway components.
source: This mechanism of XPD inhibition by MAT1 does not exclude the possibility of additional repression of NER activity by the CAK subcomplex through phosphorylation of NER pathway components (Araújo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging alternative mechanisms supported by a citation.

source: Our structure also resolves in detail the XPD-p44 interaction, a known regulatory interface (Dubaele et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2015; Kuper et al., 2014) affected by numerous disease mutations (Cleaver et al., 1999; Greber et al., 2017; Kuper et al., 2014) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

source: Our structure also resolves in detail the XPD-p44 interaction, a known regulatory interface (Dubaele et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2015; Kuper et al., 2014) affected by numerous disease mutations (Cleaver et al., 1999; Greber et al., 2017; Kuper et al., 2014) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The interaction surface between p44 and XPD is relatively small at 940 Å2.
source: The relatively small interaction surface between p44 and XPD, of just 940 Å2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), contrasts with the much larger buried surface of 3300 Å2 between XPD and p62, or 1580 Å2 for the p52-XPB interaction.
evidence: This is calculated from the structure.

claim: The smaller interaction surface between p44 and XPD may result in higher sensitivity to mutations that localize at the XPD-p44 interface.
source: This smaller interaction surface may result in higher sensitivity to mutations that localize at the XPD-p44 interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The structure rationalizes the deleterious effect of mutations L174W and T175R in the β4-α5 loop of p44.
source: Our structure, thus, rationalizes the deleterious effect of a number of natural and synthetic mutations in this interface (see Appendix 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–E), including mutations L174W and T175R in the β4-α5 loop of p44 (Figure 5E) (Kim et al., 2015; Seroz et al., 2000), which may lead to steric clashes in the densely packed interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), and the XPD R722W mutation (Kuper et al., 2014), which disrupts the salt bridge with D75 in p44 and may additionally cause steric clashes with neighboring p44 residues due to the bulky tryptophan side chain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and supported by citations.

claim: The XPD R616P, D673G, and G675R disease mutations act via disruption of the XPD structure or the XPD-p44 interface, but not via disruption of the interaction with p62.
source: Our structure also shows that, in contrast to a previously proposed model (Luo et al., 2015), the XPD R616P, D673G, and G675R disease mutations act either via disruption of the XPD structure or the XPD-p44 interface, but not via disruption of the interaction with p62 (see Appendix 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and contrasts with a previous model.

claim: The p44-dependent stimulation of XPD activity does not depend on the presence of p62.
source: Notably, the p44-dependet stimulation of XPD activity does not depend on the presence of p62 (Dubaele et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2015; Kuper et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: XP mutations mostly localize near the helicase substrate-binding or active sites.
source: Our analysis confirms that XP mutations mostly localize near the helicase substrate-binding or active sites, while TTD mutations predominantly localize to the periphery of XPD (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008), where they disrupt TFIIH assembly and cause the transcription defects that are a hallmark of this disease (Dubaele et al., 2003) (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by citations.

claim: TTD mutations predominantly localize to the periphery of XPD.
source: Our analysis confirms that XP mutations mostly localize near the helicase substrate-binding or active sites, while TTD mutations predominantly localize to the periphery of XPD (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008), where they disrupt TFIIH assembly and cause the transcription defects that are a hallmark of this disease (Dubaele et al., 2003) (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by citations.

claim: TTD mutations disrupt TFIIH assembly and cause the transcription defects that are a hallmark of this disease.
source: Our analysis confirms that XP mutations mostly localize near the helicase substrate-binding or active sites, while TTD mutations predominantly localize to the periphery of XPD (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008), where they disrupt TFIIH assembly and cause the transcription defects that are a hallmark of this disease (Dubaele et al., 2003) (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The structure reveals XPD wrapped by numerous interactions with XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1.
source: Our study reveals the complete structure of the TFIIH core complex and provides mechanistic insights into the regulation of its two component helicases. Specifically, it shows XPD wrapped by numerous interactions with XPB, p62, p44, and MAT1 (Figure 5C,D), indicating how its activity can be tightly controlled and de-repressed only when its enzymatic function is needed.
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: XPD activity can be tightly controlled and de-repressed only when its enzymatic function is needed.

claim: XPD activity is not needed and most likely inhibited during transcription initiation.
source: XPD activity is not needed and most likely inhibited during transcription initiation, but it may also be tightly controlled during NER, when repair bubble opening and lesion verification need to be coordinated with the recruitment and activation of the damage recognition and processing machinery (Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge and inference from the structure.

claim: XPD activity may be tightly controlled during NER.
source: XPD activity is not needed and most likely inhibited during transcription initiation, but it may also be tightly controlled during NER, when repair bubble opening and lesion verification need to be coordinated with the recruitment and activation of the damage recognition and processing machinery (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional requirements of NER.

claim: The structure shows how p62 is able to impede both substrate and nucleotide binding in XPD RecA1.
source: Our structure now shows how p62 is able to impede both substrate and nucleotide binding in XPD RecA1, and hints at dynamic structural changes of p62 during de-repression and enzymatic activity of XPD, possibly regulated by other components of the transcription or NER pathways.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: Dynamic structural changes of p62 may occur during de-repression and enzymatic activity of XPD.
source: Our structure now shows how p62 is able to impede both substrate and nucleotide binding in XPD RecA1, and hints at dynamic structural changes of p62 during de-repression and enzymatic activity of XPD, possibly regulated by other components of the transcription or NER pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The length of DNA fragments excised during NER is approximately 29 nt, with 22 nt located 5' and 5 nt located 3' of a thymine dimer lesion.
source: It is worth noting that the length of DNA fragments excised during NER is approx. 29 nt, with 22 nt located 5' and 5 nt located 3' of a thymine dimer lesion (Huang et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The 22 nt 5'-fragment corresponds well to the estimated 20 nt of DNA required to span the distance from the DNA damage verification pocket in XPD to the helicase elements of XPB.
source: According to our structure, the 22 nt 5'-fragment corresponds well to the estimated 20 nt of DNA that are required to span the distance from the DNA damage verification pocket in XPD (Mathieu et al., 2013) to the helicase elements of XPB.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure.

claim: It has not been fully resolved whether XPB participates in DNA translocation or unwinding during TFIIH activity in NER.
source: Additionally, it has not been fully resolved whether XPB participates in DNA translocation or unwinding during TFIIH activity in NER (Li et al., 2015), which would be required in the tracking model (Li et al., 2015), or whether it exclusively acts to anchor the complex in the vicinity of the DNA lesion (Coin et al., 2007; Oksenych et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The structural data are compatible with a model that localizes XPG near XPD and p62 (site of 3'-incision), XPF-ERCC1 near XPB (site of 5'-incision), and with RPA binding the non-damaged strand.
source: Independently of the orientation of the repair bubble, our structural data are compatible with literature data introduced above and a model (Figure 7C) that localizes XPG near XPD and p62 (site of 3'-incision), XPF-ERCC1 near XPB (site of 5'-incision), and with RPA binding the non-damaged strand (Fagbemi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structure and literature data.
